items.q: Well, after he left Nat he went with his brother's group for a while, the Four Blazers. Johnny Moore's Four Blazers. But after that he just stopped. But he was a great guitarist, he was an innovator also. And let's see.

ctx.x: Harmonically, yeah. Oscar and I, you know, we kind of thought alike. So we kind of gravitated toward eachother. Whe he'd come to town he would kind of seek me out, or if I was around him I would seek him out. And we would play and you know -- but when he left Nat he just -- it's an amazing thing. I think he stopped playing. Now, this I could never reconcile myself to this. How could a man who was that great just stop playing. You know. And he was comparatively -- at the point he stopped he was in his forties,…

Well, after he left Nat he went with his brother's group for a while, the Four Blazers. Johnny Moore's Four Blazers. But after that he just stopped. But he was a great guitarist, he was an innovator also. And let's see.

After Charlie I think Tal Farlow came through with bebop. Playing. And I think one of the great innovators of our time, and who was Wes Montgomery. Wes Montgomery in my estimation was one of the most lyrical guitarists I've ever heard. That includes everybody. He came closer to having it all as far as chords, as far as single strings, just -- he was just sheer beauty. Wes Montgomery.
